← Oxford game library

Geography: build, investigate, revise

116 activities covering 58 topics, with two practical missions in each activity. There are 29 activities in each player mode. The collection uses 10 shared interaction families, matched to the topic; these are not 116 separate simulation engines.

Run a lesson

  1. Choose Geography, grade and player mode. Open an activity and review its practice source.
  2. Edit the mission brief and expand the mission settings to change locations, cards, measurements, clues, constraints or model values. Update the brief when changing its data. Save to My lessons or download a lesson file for another device.
  3. Teams choose 2–6 names. Each team locks its response before the shared review. Two-player activities use independent simultaneous touch panels; neither panel is secret.
  4. Open Mission brief & evidence, then construct a solution. Use the compass, place and rotate map fragments, build services, test flood defences, deliver cargo, collect measurements, sculpt relief or draw an evidence artefact. Most controls support keyboard activation; freehand drawing uses touch or a mouse.
  5. Complete mission checks the constructed result. An unsuccessful test gives feedback and leaves the work editable. A successful mission starts at 100 points, with 10 points deducted per unsuccessful test, to a minimum of 20. Reset and undo do not erase those attempts. Teacher review / finish submits an unfinished mission for zero points.
  6. Discuss why the solution works. The automatic check assesses the configured model, not the quality of a student’s spoken explanation. Rotate the student at the board for whole-class activities.

Different ways to show understanding

  • Atlas reconstruction
  • Compass expedition
  • Flood defence laboratory
  • Settlement planner
  • Supply-chain challenge
  • Water-drop journey
  • Landscape sculptor
  • Geography creation studio
  • Time-travel museum
  • Fieldwork investigation

Examples include rebuilding a real atlas, navigating around obstacles, buying cooling for a perishable shipment, preparing neighbourhoods for two storms, placing clinics and water points, tracing a water-drop journey, sculpting a valley, curating a sequence of exhibits, sampling field sites and creating an evidence sketch. The creation studio requires a teacher or partner to review the geographical reasoning; its completion check only verifies that an artefact was created.

Practice sources and adaptations

The original attachment supplied ideas rather than the textbook pages, photographs, case-study datasets or climate graphs. Activities use authored practice sources and clearly labelled fictional datasets where those materials were unavailable. Replace these with your assigned evidence before assessing textbook-specific recall. Schematic grids are not navigation maps; their stated coordinates and scales belong to the exercise. Token budgets, glacier mass and sediment energy are simplified classroom models.

Physical construction, hidden partner materials, interviews and long written responses have been adapted for a public shared smartboard. Some interaction families recur across topics where they fit. The original idea and both implemented missions are shown below so teachers can judge the adaptation.

There are no multiple-choice Geography activities in this release. Older saved or imported Geography quizzes open as creation studios using their original source and model answer. The stored original remains unchanged until the teacher saves the upgraded copy. Current library entries always use the new adventures.

Research and attribution

These Oxford activities are original implementations informed by the teaching approaches below. Natural Earth provides the public-domain country outlines; other illustrations are original SVG artwork.

  • Ordnance Survey: teaching map skills: Purposeful map reconstruction, navigation and fieldwork.
  • Geographical Association: games and simulations: Resource decisions, networks, long-term consequences and evidence.
  • NOAA: Water Cycle Board Game: A water molecule journey with a recorded route through stores.
  • UNDRR: Stop Disasters: Place mitigation measures, simulate a hazard and revise a plan.
  • Royal Geographical Society: enquiry and mysteries: Construct explanations from connected evidence, with teacher review.
  • Natural Earth: public-domain map data: Atlas outlines. Our activities and artwork are independently implemented.

7A2.8 Height and contoursContour Mountain Maker
Original ideaMatch contours to profiles, construct cross-sections, and choose a route based on slope.
SoloLandscape sculptor

Construct a hillside cross-section. Drag across the rock to sculpt it. Scraping removes one unit, plucking removes two, and deposition adds one. Match the target cross-section in all four strips; the transparent height profile is your survey guide. This is a block model of relief, not a real erosion-rate simulation.
